questions.question: The primary purpose of cowl flaps is to:-

options.text: control the flow of air over the engine cylinders to maintain the correct operating temperature
direct air into the carburettor intake

questions.explanation: Cowl flaps are adjustable panels on the engine cowling that control the amount of cooling air flowing over the engine cylinders. Opening them increases airflow for cooling (used during climb); closing them reduces cooling airflow and drag (used during cruise).

questions.question: The cylinder head temperature gauge usually obtains its reading from:-

options.text: a cylinder which tests show runs the hottest
the cylinder closest to the exhaust
the cylinder closest to the carburettor

questions.explanation: The CHT gauge sensor is placed on the cylinder that testing has shown runs the hottest during normal operation. This ensures the pilot is monitoring the worst-case temperature. If this cylinder is within limits, all others should be as well.

questions.question: Engine cylinder barrels and heads are usually fitted with fins in order to:-
questions.explanation: Cooling fins increase the surface area of the cylinder barrels and heads, allowing more heat to be transferred to the cooling air flowing over them. This is essential for air-cooled engines used in most light aircraft.

questions.question: The most likely cause of the over-extension of an oleo in an undercarriage leg is:-

options.text: excessive hydraulic fluid and low air pressure

questions.explanation: An oleo strut uses compressed air (or nitrogen) and hydraulic fluid to absorb landing loads. Over-extension occurs when the air pressure is too high, pushing the strut further out than normal. Excessive fluid with low air pressure would cause under-extension.

questions.question: An over-inflated tyre may result in:-

options.text: excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre
excessive tread wear on the edges of the tyre

questions.explanation: An over-inflated tyre bulges in the centre, causing the centre of the tread to bear most of the load and wear faster. An under-inflated tyre sags, causing the edges to wear faster. Correct inflation ensures even tread wear across the full width.

questions.question: The purpose of a torque link on a nosewheel shock strut assembly is to:-

options.text: keep the nosewheel correctly aligned with the airframe
limit the extension of the oleo strut

questions.explanation: Torque links (also called scissors links) connect the upper and lower parts of the oleo strut. They allow the strut to compress and extend while preventing the lower part (and wheel) from rotating relative to the upper part, keeping the nosewheel aligned with the aircraft.

questions.question: A semi-monocoque fuselage design is one in which:-

options.text: the shape and rigidity is provided by formers and stringers whilst the stressed skin carries part of the load
aluminium tubing creates the shape whilst the stressed skin carries all the load
the skin carries all structural loads without internal framework
a truss framework carries all loads and the skin is non-structural

questions.explanation: A semi-monocoque structure uses formers (frames) to give the fuselage its shape, stringers (longitudinal members) for stiffness, and a stressed skin that carries a significant portion of the structural loads. This is the most common fuselage construction in modern light aircraft.

questions.question: The most important structural component of a wing:-
questions.explanation: The main spar is the primary load-bearing member of the wing. It runs spanwise and carries the bending loads created by lift. Ribs give the wing its aerofoil shape, and the skin (in stressed-skin construction) carries some torsional and shear loads.

questions.question: The part of a wing to which the ailerons and flaps are usually attached is the:-
questions.explanation: Ailerons and flaps are hinged to the rear (auxiliary) spar of the wing. The rear spar provides the structural attachment point for these trailing edge control surfaces and carries the hinge loads.

questions.question: Tyre creep may cause:-

options.text: the inflation valve to break away from the inner tube

questions.explanation: Tyre creep is the movement of the tyre on the wheel rim, usually caused by braking forces during landing. If the tyre slips on the rim, it can pull the inflation valve stem, potentially tearing it from the inner tube and causing rapid deflation. Creep marks on the tyre and rim are checked during pre-flight.

questions.question: A shimmy in the nosewheel whilst taxying indicates that:-

options.text: the torque links are worn or have failed
the nosewheel tyre pressure is too low
the nosewheel wheel is out of balance

questions.explanation: Nosewheel shimmy (rapid side-to-side oscillation) is most commonly caused by worn or failed torque links, which normally prevent the wheel from oscillating. Other causes include worn shimmy damper, incorrect tyre pressure, or wheel imbalance, but worn torque links are the primary cause.

questions.question: A fuselage which is constructed to allow the skin to take some of the load is:-
questions.explanation: In a semi-monocoque structure, the skin is 'stressed' — it carries a portion of the structural loads (particularly torsion and shear) in addition to the internal framework of formers and stringers. In a pure truss structure, the skin is non-structural.

questions.question: The most likely cause of the under-extension of an oleo in an undercarriage leg is:-

options.text: worn seals allowing air to escape

questions.explanation: Under-extension of an oleo strut occurs when the air (or nitrogen) pressure is too low. The compressed gas is what extends the strut; insufficient pressure means the strut cannot fully extend. This is checked during pre-flight by observing the visible chrome portion of the strut.

questions.question: Tyre creep may be expected to occur:-

options.text: only when brakes are applied harshly

questions.explanation: Tyre creep occurs during normal landing when the stationary tyre contacts the runway and is suddenly spun up to ground speed. The friction force between the tyre and runway can cause the tyre to slip on the rim. Heavy braking can also contribute.

questions.question: In a Truss, or Girder-type fuselage the main structural component is a:-
questions.explanation: In a truss (girder) fuselage, longerons are the main longitudinal members that carry the primary loads. They run the length of the fuselage and are connected by cross-bracing (struts and wires) to form a rigid framework. The skin in a truss structure is typically non-structural fabric or light sheet metal.

questions.question: The timing of the ignition of the fuel and air mixture in an internal combustion engine is arranged to occur:-

options.text: between 20° and 25° before TDC during the compression stroke
at TDC during the compression stroke
after TDC during the power stroke
at BDC during the induction stroke

questions.explanation: Ignition occurs before TDC (top dead centre) to allow time for the flame front to develop and reach maximum pressure just after TDC, when the piston begins the power stroke. This advance timing (20-25° BTDC) ensures maximum power is extracted from the combustion event.

questions.question: A condition which may occur in only one cylinder of an engine as a result of too lean a mixture is:-
questions.explanation: Pre-ignition is the ignition of the fuel/air mixture by a hot spot (such as an overheated exhaust valve or carbon deposit) before the spark plug fires. A lean mixture burns hotter, creating hot spots. It can occur in individual cylinders because mixture distribution is not perfectly even across all cylinders.

questions.question: Valve overlap in the four stroke engine will occur between the:-
questions.explanation: Valve overlap is the brief period when both the exhaust valve (closing) and the inlet valve (opening) are open simultaneously. This occurs at the transition between the exhaust and induction strokes (near TDC). It helps scavenge remaining exhaust gases and improves cylinder filling.

questions.question: In a piston engine, the piston will have passed BDC and be moving towards TDC during:-
questions.explanation: The four strokes are: Induction (TDC→BDC), Compression (BDC→TDC), Power (TDC→BDC), Exhaust (BDC→TDC). The piston moves from BDC toward TDC during the compression stroke (compressing the mixture) and the exhaust stroke (expelling burnt gases).

questions.question: The type of pump utilised in a piston engine to provide high pressure oil lubrication is a:-
questions.explanation: A gear-type pump uses two meshing gears to trap and pressurize oil. It is the standard type used in aircraft piston engines for the pressure lubrication system because it provides a reliable, consistent flow of oil at the required pressure.

questions.question: Lubrication of the main bearings and crankshaft of the engine is provided:-

options.text: by both high pressure oil and splash lubrication

questions.explanation: Main bearings and the crankshaft receive oil under pressure from the gear pump through drilled passages. Additionally, splash lubrication occurs as the crankshaft and connecting rods dip into or throw oil around the crankcase, lubricating cylinder walls and other components.

questions.question: Dry sump piston engine lubrication systems make use of a scavenge pump to:-

options.text: pump oil from the sump back to the oil tank
pump oil from the tank to the engine
filter the oil before it reaches the engine

questions.explanation: In a dry sump system, oil is stored in a separate tank rather than in the engine sump. The scavenge pump (which has a greater capacity than the pressure pump) continuously removes oil from the sump and returns it to the external tank, keeping the sump 'dry'.

questions.question: In a wet sump piston engine lubrication system:-

options.text: oil is stored in the engine sump and distributed by a pressure pump
oil is stored in an external tank
oil is distributed by gravity only
a scavenge pump returns oil to an external reservoir

questions.explanation: In a wet sump system, the oil reservoir is the engine sump (bottom of the crankcase). A gear-type pressure pump draws oil from the sump and distributes it under pressure to the engine components. This is simpler and lighter than a dry sump system.

questions.question: A high oil temperature coupled with low oil pressure:-

options.text: are an indication of low oil supply
indicates the oil cooler is blocked
indicates the oil is too thick

questions.explanation: High oil temperature with low oil pressure is a serious warning indicating insufficient oil in the system. Low oil quantity means less oil to absorb and dissipate heat (temperature rises) and less oil for the pump to pressurize (pressure drops). This requires immediate action — reduce power and land as soon as practicable.

questions.question: The purpose of the pressure relief valve in a lubrication system is to:-

options.text: maintain a constant oil pressure over a range of engine power changes
control the pressure of oil between the pump and filter

questions.explanation: The pressure relief valve opens when oil pressure exceeds a set value, bypassing excess oil back to the sump or inlet side of the pump. This maintains a relatively constant oil pressure regardless of engine RPM changes, protecting the system from excessive pressure.

questions.question: The temperature of the oil in a wet sump lubrication system is usually measured:-
questions.explanation: Oil temperature is measured after the oil cooler so the pilot can monitor the temperature of the oil actually being delivered to the engine components. This gives the most useful indication of the oil's ability to provide adequate lubrication.

questions.question: The function of the distributor in a magneto is to:-

options.text: provide high voltage to the spark plugs in the correct firing order

questions.explanation: The distributor in a magneto directs the high voltage pulse from the secondary winding to the correct spark plug in the proper firing sequence. It is a rotating contact that connects to each spark plug lead in turn as the engine rotates.

questions.question: The purpose of baffles in an aircraft's fuel tank is to:-

options.text: prevent the fuel from surging about during flight

questions.explanation: Baffles are internal partitions within the fuel tank that restrict the movement of fuel during manoeuvres, turbulence, and attitude changes. Without baffles, fuel surging could cause sudden CG shifts, unporting of the fuel pickup, and structural loads on the tank walls.

questions.question: The purpose of an impulse coupling in a magneto is to:-

options.text: produce a strong retarded spark for easier engine starting
increase the magneto output during cruise
prevent the engine from running backwards

questions.explanation: An impulse coupling is a spring-loaded mechanism fitted to one magneto (usually the left). During starting, it momentarily holds and then releases the magneto, spinning it rapidly to produce a strong spark. It also retards the timing to prevent kickback during hand-propping or starter engagement.

questions.question: The electrical current produced by a magneto:-

options.text: is created by a rotating magnet
is supplied by the aircraft battery

questions.explanation: A magneto is a self-contained ignition system that generates its own electrical current using a rotating permanent magnet. This is why the engine can continue to run even with the battery and master switch off — the magneto is independent of the aircraft electrical system.

questions.question: If the earth wire from a magneto to the aircraft structure is broken:-

options.text: the engine will continue to run with the magneto switch in the off position
the magneto will produce a weaker spark

questions.explanation: The magneto switch works by grounding (earthing) the magneto to stop it. If the earth wire is broken, the magneto cannot be grounded and will continue to produce sparks regardless of switch position. This is a serious safety hazard — the propeller should always be treated as live.

questions.question: The fuel supply line from the fuel tank to the engine normally:-

options.text: draws fuel from a position higher than the sump drain to allow impurities to settle
draws fuel from the very bottom of the tank
draws fuel from the top of the tank
draws fuel from the centre of the tank

questions.explanation: The fuel pickup is positioned slightly above the lowest point (sump) of the tank. Water and other contaminants, being heavier than fuel, settle to the bottom of the sump below the pickup. This prevents contaminated fuel from reaching the engine. The sump drain allows these contaminants to be drained during pre-flight.

questions.question: The presence of carburettor icing would be indicated by:-

options.text: the engine starting to run rough and a decrease in RPM
a decrease in fuel flow only

questions.explanation: Carburettor ice restricts the airflow through the venturi, leaning the mixture and reducing power. In a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft, this shows as a decrease in RPM and rough running. In a CSU-equipped aircraft, it shows as a decrease in manifold pressure with RPM maintained by the CSU.

questions.question: When the throttle is opened quickly, the throttle accelerator pump will:-

options.text: discharge additional fuel into the venturi
increase the air flow through the carburettor

questions.explanation: The accelerator pump is a mechanical pump linked to the throttle. When the throttle is opened rapidly, it squirts extra fuel into the venturi to prevent a momentary lean condition. Without it, the sudden increase in airflow would temporarily lean the mixture, causing hesitation or backfiring.

questions.question: An accelerator pump is often incorporated in a carburettor in order to:-

options.text: provide extra fuel when the throttle is opened rapidly
increase the fuel supply during high power operation

questions.explanation: The accelerator pump provides a brief burst of extra fuel when the throttle is opened quickly. This compensates for the lag in fuel metering — air responds to throttle changes faster than fuel, so without the pump, a rapid throttle opening would cause a momentary lean condition.

questions.question: An engine which starts to run rough and then slowly loses power is probably suffering from:-
questions.explanation: Carburettor icing causes a gradual restriction of airflow. The engine first runs rough as the mixture becomes progressively leaner, then slowly loses power as ice builds up further. Applying carburettor heat should restore power (after an initial further roughness as the ice melts).

questions.question: When leaning the fuel/air mixture:-

options.text: the ratio of fuel to air is reduced
the ratio of fuel to air is increased
only the air flow is changed

questions.explanation: Leaning reduces the amount of fuel relative to air in the mixture. This is done at altitude where the air is less dense — the carburettor delivers the same amount of fuel but less air mass, making the mixture too rich. Leaning restores the correct fuel-to-air ratio for efficient combustion.

questions.question: The application of carburettor heat:-

options.text: will richen the mixture because of the higher air temperature
has no effect on the mixture

questions.explanation: Carburettor heat directs warm air (heated by the exhaust manifold) into the carburettor. Warm air is less dense, so less air mass enters the engine while the same amount of fuel is metered. This richens the mixture and causes a slight drop in RPM/power. It also reduces the risk of icing.

questions.question: Carburettor icing is most likely to occur:-

options.text: at the venturi and butterfly valve

questions.explanation: Ice forms at the venturi (where air accelerates and temperature drops due to the Venturi effect) and at the butterfly valve (throttle valve) where fuel evaporation causes further cooling. These two areas can experience temperature drops of 20-30°C, causing ice to form even in ambient temperatures up to +25°C.

questions.question: The blade angle of a propeller varies from hub to tip in order to:-

options.text: ensure that the thrust produced is approximately constant along the blade
reduce the weight of the propeller

questions.explanation: The tip of the propeller moves faster than the hub. To maintain a constant angle of attack (and therefore constant thrust) along the blade, the blade angle must be greater at the hub and decrease toward the tip. This twist ensures efficient thrust production across the entire blade.

questions.question: The correct sequence for increasing power in an aeroplane with a Constant Speed Unit (CSU) is:-

options.text: richen the mixture, increase the RPM, then increase the manifold pressure
increase the manifold pressure, increase the RPM, then richen the mixture
increase the RPM, increase the manifold pressure, then richen the mixture
increase the manifold pressure, richen the mixture, then increase the RPM

questions.explanation: When increasing power with a CSU: (1) Richen mixture first to ensure adequate fuel for higher power, (2) Increase RPM (prop lever forward) to handle the increased manifold pressure, (3) Increase manifold pressure (throttle forward). This sequence prevents overboosting. When reducing power, reverse the order.

questions.question: During take-off in an aeroplane equipped with a Constant Speed Unit (CSU), it would be most beneficial to have:-

options.text: the blade angle at cruise setting

questions.explanation: A small (fine) blade angle allows the engine to develop high RPM and maximum power at low forward speed — ideal for take-off. A large (coarse) blade angle is more efficient at cruise speed. Think of it like low gear in a car for starting, high gear for cruising.

questions.question: If an aeroplane with a fixed pitch propeller is placed in a shallow dive so that forward speed increases with no change in power setting, the RPM will:-
questions.explanation: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the blade angle cannot change. As forward speed increases in a dive, the angle of attack of the propeller blade decreases, reducing the aerodynamic load on the blade. The engine can spin faster with less resistance, so RPM increases.

questions.question: After starting an engine, black smoke is seen coming from the exhaust. This indicates:-

options.text: that the mixture is too rich
that the mixture is too lean

questions.explanation: Black smoke from the exhaust indicates incomplete combustion due to an excessively rich mixture — there is too much fuel for the available air. This is common immediately after starting (due to priming) and should clear as the engine warms up and the mixture is leaned.

questions.question: An operational advantage of the alternator is that it:-

options.text: will still produce electrical power at low RPM
will generate a DC supply without using a rectifier
does not require a voltage regulator

questions.explanation: An alternator produces useful electrical output at lower RPM than a generator. This is important because it means the electrical system can charge the battery and power equipment even at idle RPM. A generator requires higher RPM to produce adequate output.

questions.question: The correct level of electrolyte in a lead acid battery should be maintained by the addition of:-
questions.explanation: Only distilled water should be added to a lead-acid battery. During charging, water evaporates but the acid does not. Adding acid would increase the acid concentration and damage the battery. Tap water contains minerals that would contaminate the electrolyte.

questions.question: One of the advantages of refuelling an aeroplane with full tanks after flight is that:-

options.text: full tanks will minimise condensation forming overnight
the stain from fuel leaks will be more easily noticed
it reduces the risk of fuel contamination
it is easier to check the fuel quantity

questions.explanation: Filling tanks after flight minimises the air space above the fuel. Overnight temperature drops cause moisture in this air to condense as water droplets, which contaminate the fuel. Full tanks leave minimal air space, greatly reducing condensation and water contamination.

questions.question: One of the benefits of the DC generator is that it:-

options.text: does not rely on battery power to bring it on line
will continue to produce power at low speeds
is more efficient than an alternator at all speeds

questions.explanation: A DC generator is self-exciting — it uses residual magnetism in its field windings to start generating. It does not need battery power to initiate output. An alternator, by contrast, requires battery power to energise its field coils before it can produce output.

questions.question: Control of the voltage output from a DC generator is achieved through a:-
questions.explanation: A voltage regulator controls the generator's output voltage by varying the current flowing through the field windings. As engine RPM changes, the regulator adjusts the field current to maintain a constant voltage output (typically 14V for a 12V system or 28V for a 24V system).

questions.question: The use of fuel with a lower octane rating than that recommended by the aircraft manufacturer may lead to:-
questions.explanation: Octane rating measures a fuel's resistance to detonation (spontaneous, uncontrolled combustion). Lower octane fuel detonates more easily under the high compression and temperatures in the engine. Detonation causes severe engine damage including piston and cylinder damage, and must be avoided.

questions.question: The storage capacity of a battery is usually expressed in:-
questions.explanation: Battery capacity is measured in ampere-hours (Ah). A 35Ah battery can theoretically deliver 35 amps for one hour, or 1 amp for 35 hours. This tells the pilot how long the battery can power the electrical system without the alternator/generator running.

questions.question: A rectifier is required in an alternator in order to:-

options.text: convert the AC output into DC

questions.explanation: An alternator inherently produces alternating current (AC). Aircraft electrical systems use direct current (DC), so a rectifier (typically a diode bridge) is built into the alternator to convert the AC output to DC before it enters the aircraft electrical bus.

questions.question: A reverse current cut-out relay in a generator-supplied electrical system is used to:-

options.text: prevent the flow of current from the battery to the generator
protect the circuit from being overloaded

questions.explanation: When the generator output drops below battery voltage (e.g., at low RPM), current would flow from the battery into the generator, potentially damaging it and draining the battery. The reverse current cut-out relay disconnects the generator from the bus when this condition is detected.

questions.question: The purpose of the engine driven vacuum pump used in an aircraft's gyroscopic instrument system is to:-

options.text: decrease the pressure within the instrument case
pump high pressure air onto the gyro rotor
provide electrical power to the gyros

questions.explanation: The vacuum pump creates a low pressure (suction) inside the instrument case. Filtered air is drawn in through jets directed at the gyro rotor buckets, spinning the rotor at high speed (typically 10,000-15,000 RPM). The air then exits through the vacuum pump.

questions.question: Over-speeding of vacuum driven gyro rotors is prevented by:-

options.text: a pressure relief valve located just before the vacuum pump
a governor on the gyro rotor
a speed limiter in the vacuum pump

questions.explanation: A suction relief valve (pressure relief valve) is installed in the vacuum line before the pump. It allows ambient air to enter the system if the suction becomes too great, limiting the maximum vacuum and preventing the gyro rotors from spinning too fast, which could damage the instruments.

questions.question: The suction required to operate vacuum driven gyroscopes is usually between:-
questions.explanation: Vacuum-driven gyroscopic instruments (attitude indicator and heading indicator) require a suction of approximately 3-5 inches of mercury (inHg) to spin the gyro rotors at the correct speed. This is monitored by a suction gauge on the instrument panel.

questions.question: A left-zero ammeter is incorporated in an electrical system to:-

options.text: indicate the flow of current from the alternator
indicate the flow of current into and out of the battery
measure the voltage in the system

questions.explanation: A left-zero (loadmeter) ammeter shows the total current output from the alternator/generator. Zero is at the left, and the needle deflects right to show current being produced. If the alternator fails, the needle drops to zero. This differs from a centre-zero ammeter which shows battery charge/discharge.

questions.question: The instruments that would be affected by a static vent blockage are:-

options.text: the altimeter, airspeed indicator, and vertical speed indicator
the altimeter and vertical speed indicator only
the attitude indicator and heading indicator

questions.explanation: All three pitot-static instruments use static pressure: the altimeter (static only), the VSI (static only), and the ASI (pitot minus static). A blocked static vent will cause errors in all three instruments. Gyroscopic instruments are not affected as they use the vacuum system.

questions.question: If the alternate static vent, located in the cockpit, is opened in flight, the altimeter will:-

options.text: over-read because the cockpit pressure is usually lower than outside pressure

questions.explanation: Cockpit pressure is slightly lower than outside static pressure due to aerodynamic suction effects on the fuselage. When the alternate static source draws from the cockpit, the altimeter senses a lower pressure than actual, causing it to indicate a higher altitude than the aircraft is actually at.

questions.question: A blockage of the static vent during a descent would cause the ASI to:-
questions.explanation: The ASI measures the difference between pitot and static pressure. If the static vent is blocked during a descent, the trapped static pressure remains at the higher altitude (lower pressure). As the aircraft descends into higher actual static pressure, the pitot pressure increases but the reference static doesn't — so the indicated difference is too large, causing the ASI to over-read.

questions.question: If, during a descent, the static vent becomes blocked the altimeter will:-

options.text: continue to indicate the altitude at which the blockage occurred

questions.explanation: The altimeter measures static pressure only. If the static vent is blocked, the pressure inside the instrument case remains at the value when the blockage occurred. The altimeter will continue to show that altitude regardless of actual altitude changes — it effectively becomes a fixed reading.

questions.question: If, during level flight, the static vent becomes blocked the ASI reading will:-

options.text: remain constant as long as the aircraft remains at the same altitude and speed

questions.explanation: In level flight at constant speed, both pitot pressure and static pressure remain constant. If the static vent blocks, the trapped static pressure is the same as the actual static pressure (since altitude hasn't changed). The ASI will read correctly as long as speed and altitude don't change.

questions.question: In a simple airspeed indicator, pitot pressure is fed to:-

options.text: both the capsule and the case
neither — it uses static pressure only

questions.explanation: In an ASI, pitot (total) pressure is fed to the inside of the capsule, and static pressure fills the instrument case. The capsule expands or contracts based on the difference between pitot and static pressure (dynamic pressure = ½ρV²), which is proportional to airspeed.

questions.question: The basic principle of operation of an airspeed indicator is to measure the differential between:-
questions.explanation: The ASI works by measuring the difference between pitot (total) pressure and static pressure. This difference is dynamic pressure (q = ½ρV²), which is directly related to airspeed. Pitot pressure = static pressure + dynamic pressure, so dynamic pressure = pitot - static.

questions.question: As altitude is increased the capsule inside an altimeter will:-

options.text: expand, causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
contract, causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
expand, causing the instrument to show a decrease in altitude

questions.explanation: The altimeter contains an evacuated (aneroid) capsule inside a sealed case connected to the static port. As altitude increases, static pressure decreases. The capsule expands because the internal reference pressure is now greater than the surrounding static pressure. This expansion is mechanically linked to the altitude display.

questions.question: The two properties associated with a spinning gyroscope are:-
questions.explanation: Rigidity in space means the gyro maintains its orientation regardless of how the aircraft moves around it. Precession means that when a force is applied to a spinning gyro, the effect is felt 90° later in the direction of rotation. Both properties are essential for gyroscopic instruments.

questions.question: With reference to the Attitude Indicator, as an aircraft changes its pitch attitude or bank:-

options.text: the gyro remains in the vertical relative to the earth
the gyro remains at right angles to the aircraft's longitudinal axis
the gyro tilts with the aircraft
the gyro precesses to a new position

questions.explanation: The attitude indicator uses an earth gyro (vertical axis, spinning in the horizontal plane). Due to rigidity in space, the gyro remains aligned with the earth's vertical regardless of aircraft attitude changes. The aircraft moves around the gyro, and this relative movement is displayed as pitch and bank indications.

questions.question: The gyroscope used in a direction indicator is a:-

options.text: free gyro with no axis preference

questions.explanation: The direction indicator (DI/heading indicator) uses a horizontal axis gyro — the rotor spins about a horizontal axis. Due to rigidity in space, it maintains its orientation and provides a stable heading reference. It must be periodically aligned with the magnetic compass because it has no magnetic sensing capability.

questions.question: Apparent wander in a Direction Indicator is caused by:-
questions.explanation: Apparent wander (drift) occurs because the DI gyro maintains its orientation in space while the earth rotates beneath it. The rate of apparent wander depends on latitude — maximum at the poles (15°/hour) and zero at the equator. This is why the DI must be realigned with the compass every 15-20 minutes.

questions.question: Wear in the bearings and gimbals as well as air turbulence will have the effect of:-

options.text: causing real wander of a gyro

questions.explanation: Real wander is the actual physical displacement of the gyro axis caused by mechanical imperfections — bearing friction, gimbal friction, and external forces like air turbulence. Unlike apparent wander (caused by earth rotation), real wander is random and unpredictable. It contributes to the need for regular DI realignment.

questions.question: The indications on a turn indicator during a turn to the right whilst taxying are:-

options.text: the ball moves to the left and the needle shows a right turn
the ball moves to the right and the needle shows a right turn
the ball stays centred and the needle shows a right turn
the ball moves to the left and the needle shows a left turn

questions.explanation: During a ground turn (taxying), there is no bank angle — the aircraft is flat. The turn needle correctly shows the direction of turn (right). The ball, however, is thrown outward by centrifugal force (to the left in a right turn) because there is no bank to counteract it. This is normal during ground operations.

questions.question: The turn indicator makes use of a:-
questions.explanation: The turn indicator uses a rate gyro — a gyro that is restrained by a spring so that it measures the rate of turn rather than maintaining a fixed position in space. The gyro precesses proportionally to the rate of yaw, and the spring returns it to centre when the turn stops.

questions.question: Control of the precession of the gyro in a turn indicator is achieved by:-

options.text: the tension of a spring mounted between the gimbal and the case
the weight of the gyro rotor

questions.explanation: A calibrated spring connects the gyro gimbal to the instrument case. When the aircraft yaws, the gyro precesses against the spring. The spring tension controls the amount of precession for a given rate of turn, ensuring the needle deflection is proportional to the turn rate. When the turn stops, the spring returns the gyro to its neutral position.

questions.question: The needle of a turn co-ordinator shows:-
questions.explanation: Despite the miniature aircraft symbol suggesting bank angle, the turn coordinator actually shows the rate of turn (and initially the rate of roll). The gyro is canted at approximately 30° so it senses both yaw and roll rates. A standard rate turn (Rate 1) is indicated when the wing tip aligns with the index mark.

questions.question: The type of gyro used in an attitude indicator is:-
questions.explanation: The attitude indicator uses an earth gyro (also called a vertical gyro). The rotor spins about a vertical axis and is maintained in the vertical by an erection mechanism. This provides a stable reference to the earth's horizon, allowing the instrument to display pitch and bank attitude.

questions.question: During take-off the error which may be expected from an air-driven Attitude Indicator is:-

options.text: a temporary error in both pitch and roll

questions.explanation: During the acceleration of take-off, the pendulous vanes of the erection mechanism are displaced by the acceleration force. This causes the gyro to precess, resulting in temporary errors in both pitch (showing a slight climb) and roll indications. The errors correct themselves once acceleration stops.

questions.question: During flight the gyro in a Direction Indicator aligns itself with:-
questions.explanation: The DI gyro maintains its orientation relative to a fixed point in space due to gyroscopic rigidity. It has no magnetic sensing capability, so it does not align with magnetic or true north. The pilot must manually align it with the magnetic compass and periodically re-check the alignment.

questions.question: An aircraft engine is designed to operate on a specific octane rating. Using fuel of a higher octane than recommended may result in:-

options.text: lead fouling of the spark plugs

questions.explanation: Higher octane aviation fuel contains more tetraethyl lead (TEL) as an anti-knock additive. Using fuel with a higher octane rating than required means excess lead, which can deposit on spark plugs (lead fouling), reducing their effectiveness and causing misfiring.

questions.question: When attempting to start an engine which has been over-primed or flooded:-

options.text: the mixture should be in the full lean position until the engine fires, then richened slowly
continue cranking with full rich mixture
wait 30 minutes before attempting to start again

questions.explanation: A flooded engine has too much fuel in the cylinders. Setting the mixture to idle cut-off (full lean) while cranking allows the excess fuel to be drawn through and burned off without adding more fuel. Once the engine fires, the mixture is slowly moved to rich to keep it running.

questions.question: In the southern hemisphere, an aircraft maintaining a constant heading of 090° (M) on a magnetic compass — if speed is increased, the compass would:-

options.text: show an apparent turn to the south
show an apparent turn to the north
show an apparent turn to the east

questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, acceleration on an easterly or westerly heading causes the compass to show an apparent turn toward the nearer pole (south). This is because the acceleration displaces the compass magnet assembly, causing a false indication. The memory aid is SAND (South, Accelerate, North, Decelerate) — reversed for the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.question: The deviation error found in a magnetic compass:-

options.text: is caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft
is caused by the rotation of the earth
is caused by the difference between true and magnetic north

questions.explanation: Deviation is caused by magnetic fields within the aircraft — from electrical equipment, metal structures, and wiring. These local fields deflect the compass from magnetic north. Deviation varies with heading and is minimised by a compass swing (adjustment) and recorded on a deviation card in the cockpit.

questions.question: Compass deviation in a particular aircraft:-

options.text: is a fixed value for all headings

questions.explanation: Deviation changes with heading because the aircraft's magnetic fields interact differently with the earth's magnetic field depending on the aircraft's orientation. The deviation card in the cockpit lists the deviation for various headings (typically every 30°) so the pilot can apply the correct correction.

questions.question: During a descent the pressure in the capsule of a vertical speed indicator (VSI) will:-
questions.explanation: The VSI capsule is connected directly to the static port. During a descent, static pressure increases (higher pressure at lower altitude). This increased pressure is immediately felt inside the capsule. The case pressure changes more slowly through the calibrated leak, creating the differential that indicates rate of descent.

questions.question: During a climb the pressure inside the case of a vertical speed indicator (VSI) will:-

options.text: decrease at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
decrease at the same rate as the pressure within the capsule

questions.explanation: During a climb, static pressure decreases. The capsule pressure drops immediately (direct static connection), but the case pressure decreases more slowly because air must leak out through the calibrated restrictor (metering unit). This pressure differential between capsule and case indicates the rate of climb.

questions.question: Application of 'alternate air' in a fuel injection system:-

options.text: feeds air from within the engine cowling to the induction system
routes filtered air to the exhaust pipes for heating
increases the air pressure in the induction system

questions.explanation: Fuel-injected engines use 'alternate air' instead of carburettor heat. When selected, it draws unfiltered air from inside the engine cowling (which is warmed by engine heat) rather than through the normal filtered air intake. This is used if the normal intake becomes blocked by ice or debris.

questions.question: An aircraft's pitot tube is usually mounted:-

options.text: on top of the vertical fin

questions.explanation: The pitot tube must face directly into the undisturbed relative airflow to accurately measure total (pitot) pressure. It is typically mounted on the wing leading edge or on a mast projecting forward from the fuselage, away from areas of disturbed airflow.

questions.question: Normal static pressure is taken from:-

options.text: a port located in an area of undisturbed air
a tube mounted facing into the relative airflow

questions.explanation: Static ports are flush-mounted openings on the fuselage skin, positioned in an area where the air pressure is as close to undisturbed atmospheric pressure as possible. Many aircraft have two static ports (one on each side) to cancel out any position error caused by sideslip.

questions.question: The effect of having two static vents located one on either side of an aircraft's fuselage is that:-

options.text: the instruments will be more sensitive
the system will work at higher altitudes
only one vent is used at a time

questions.explanation: During sideslip or in crosswinds, one side of the fuselage experiences higher pressure and the other lower pressure. Having static ports on both sides averages these pressures, significantly reducing position error and providing a more accurate static pressure reading.

questions.question: The alternate static valve draws air from:-

options.text: an external port on the tail

questions.explanation: The alternate static source is located inside the cockpit. If the external static ports become blocked (by ice, insects, etc.), the pilot can open the alternate static valve to use cockpit pressure as a substitute. Cockpit pressure is slightly lower than outside, causing small instrument errors.

questions.question: If the speed of an aeroplane fitted with a fixed pitch propeller decreases, but the throttle setting remains constant, the RPM will:-
questions.explanation: With a fixed-pitch propeller, as forward speed decreases, the angle of attack of the propeller blades increases. This increases the aerodynamic load (drag) on the blades, and the engine cannot maintain the same RPM against the increased load, so RPM decreases.

questions.question: The component of a hydraulic system which stores hydraulic fluid under pressure is called:-
questions.explanation: An accumulator stores hydraulic fluid under pressure (using compressed gas or a spring). It provides an emergency reserve of pressurised fluid, dampens pressure surges, and supplements the pump during peak demand periods (e.g., gear retraction).

questions.question: Loss of pressure in a hydraulic system is indicated to the pilot by:-
questions.explanation: A red warning light on the instrument panel alerts the pilot to low hydraulic pressure. This is critical because hydraulic systems operate landing gear, brakes, and sometimes flaps. Some aircraft also have a hydraulic pressure gauge for monitoring.

questions.question: In the event that a fuse in an electrical circuit has blown:-

options.text: it should be replaced only once with a fuse of the same rating
it should be replaced with a fuse of a higher rating
the circuit should be left open
any available fuse can be used as a temporary replacement

questions.explanation: A blown fuse indicates an overcurrent condition. Replace it once with a fuse of the same rating. If it blows again, there is a fault in the circuit that must be investigated — do not replace it again or use a higher-rated fuse, as this could cause a fire or damage equipment.

questions.question: In the event that a circuit breaker in an electrical circuit has tripped:-

options.text: it should be pushed back in only once after allowing a cooling off period
it should be held in with tape
the master switch should be turned off

questions.explanation: A tripped circuit breaker indicates an overcurrent. Allow a brief cooling period, then reset it once. If it trips again, leave it out — there is a fault in the circuit. Never hold a circuit breaker in or bypass it, as this removes the overcurrent protection and could cause a fire.

questions.question: A hydraulic system operates on the basic principle that:-

options.text: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
fluid flows from high pressure to low pressure
fluid can be compressed to store energy

questions.explanation: Pascal's Law states that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions. This allows a small force applied at a pump to create a large force at an actuator by using different piston areas, enabling the operation of heavy components like landing gear.

questions.question: The pilot of an aircraft equipped with a manifold pressure gauge would identify carburettor icing by:-
questions.explanation: In a CSU-equipped aircraft, the constant speed unit maintains RPM by adjusting blade angle. Carburettor ice restricts airflow, reducing the power the engine can produce. This shows as a decrease in manifold pressure while RPM remains constant (maintained by the CSU). In a fixed-pitch aircraft, RPM would decrease instead.

questions.question: The effect of slats is to:-

options.text: allow the aeroplane to fly at a higher angle of attack and a lower airspeed

questions.explanation: Leading edge slats create a slot between the slat and the main wing. At high AoA, high-energy air flows through this slot over the upper surface, energising the boundary layer and delaying separation. This increases the critical AoA, allowing the aircraft to fly slower without stalling.

questions.question: When executing a turn from 160° through south to 210° in the southern hemisphere using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out on would be:-
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, the compass leads (reads ahead) when turning through south. The pilot must roll out before the compass shows the desired heading. For a turn through south to 210°, rolling out at approximately 190° on the compass will result in the aircraft actually being on 210° when the compass settles.

questions.question: In comparison to a generator, the power output of an alternator will be:-

options.text: the same at all RPM ranges

questions.explanation: An alternator produces useful output at lower RPM than a generator because it uses a rotating field (electromagnet) rather than a rotating armature. The alternator's output increases more rapidly with RPM and reaches useful levels at engine idle speed, unlike a generator which needs higher RPM.

questions.question: The presence of black oily deposits in the firing end cavity of a spark plug would probably indicate:-

options.text: that oil is slipping past the piston rings and being burnt in the combustion chamber
that the engine has been operated with too rich a mixture

questions.explanation: Black oily deposits on spark plugs indicate oil contamination in the combustion chamber. This is typically caused by worn piston rings or valve guides allowing oil to enter the cylinder. The oil burns incompletely, leaving black oily residue. This requires maintenance attention.

questions.question: The four strokes of a piston engine in the correct order are:-
questions.explanation: The four-stroke cycle (Otto cycle) is: (1) Induction — piston moves down, drawing in fuel/air mixture, (2) Compression — piston moves up, compressing the mixture, (3) Power — spark ignites mixture, expanding gases push piston down, (4) Exhaust — piston moves up, expelling burnt gases. Two crankshaft revolutions per cycle.

questions.question: The purpose of having two independent magneto ignition systems on an aircraft engine is to:-

options.text: provide redundancy and improve combustion efficiency
allow the engine to run on one magneto during cruise

questions.explanation: Dual magnetos provide safety redundancy — if one fails, the engine continues to run on the other. Additionally, two spark plugs per cylinder (one from each magneto) ignite the mixture from two points, giving more complete and efficient combustion. Running on one magneto causes a slight RPM drop (typically 50-75 RPM).

questions.question: During the magneto check before take-off, an excessive RPM drop on one magneto indicates:-

options.text: a fault in that magneto or its associated spark plugs

questions.explanation: During the magneto check, switching from BOTH to a single magneto should cause a small RPM drop (typically 50-175 RPM depending on aircraft type). An excessive drop indicates a problem with the other magneto system — faulty magneto, fouled spark plugs, or broken ignition leads. The aircraft should not be flown until the fault is rectified.

questions.question: During the magneto check, if there is NO RPM drop when switching from BOTH to a single magneto, this indicates:-

options.text: a possible fault — the other magneto may not be firing or the P-lead may be broken
the engine is in excellent condition
the propeller is at the correct pitch

questions.explanation: No RPM drop is abnormal and potentially dangerous. It could mean the other magneto was already not firing (so switching it off makes no difference), or the P-lead (earth wire) is broken, meaning that magneto cannot be switched off. This is a serious safety concern and must be investigated before flight.

questions.question: Detonation in an aircraft engine differs from pre-ignition in that:-

options.text: detonation is the spontaneous explosion of the unburnt mixture ahead of the flame front
detonation occurs before the spark plug fires
pre-ignition is caused by low octane fuel
detonation only occurs at low power settings

questions.explanation: Detonation occurs after normal ignition — the remaining unburnt mixture spontaneously explodes rather than burning progressively. Pre-ignition occurs before the spark — a hot spot ignites the mixture prematurely. Both are destructive, but they are different phenomena. Detonation is caused by low octane fuel, high manifold pressure, or lean mixture at high power.

questions.question: The colour coding for 100LL aviation gasoline is:-
questions.explanation: 100LL (100 octane Low Lead) aviation gasoline is dyed blue. The colour coding helps prevent misfuelling: 100LL = blue, 100/130 = green, 80/87 = red, Jet A-1 = clear/straw. Using the wrong fuel type can cause engine damage or failure.

questions.question: The purpose of draining fuel from the fuel tank sumps during pre-flight is to:-

options.text: check for water contamination and sediment
reduce the fuel load for take-off

questions.explanation: Water is heavier than aviation fuel and settles to the bottom of the tank sump. Draining a sample from each sump allows the pilot to visually check for water (clear bubbles at the bottom of the blue fuel), sediment, or incorrect fuel type. This is a critical pre-flight check.

questions.question: The fuel/air mixture ratio for best power is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The chemically correct (stoichiometric) ratio is approximately 1:15 by weight. Best power mixture is slightly richer at about 1:12. Best economy mixture is slightly leaner at about 1:16. The mixture must be within the flammability range of approximately 1:8 (rich limit) to 1:20 (lean limit).

questions.question: The master switch in an aircraft controls:-

options.text: the connection of the battery and alternator/generator to the electrical bus
the fuel supply to the engine

questions.explanation: The master switch connects the battery and alternator/generator to the aircraft electrical bus. It typically has two halves — a battery switch and an alternator switch. Turning off the master switch disconnects all electrical power except the magneto ignition system, which is self-powered.

questions.question: If the alternator fails in flight, the pilot should:-

options.text: reduce the electrical load to essential items and plan to land as soon as practicable
switch off the battery to conserve power

questions.explanation: With the alternator failed, the battery is the sole source of electrical power and has limited capacity. The pilot should shed non-essential electrical loads (lights, radios not needed, etc.) to extend battery life, and plan to land as soon as practicable. The engine will continue to run normally as the magnetos are independent.

questions.question: A centre-zero ammeter indicates:-

options.text: the rate of charge or discharge of the battery
the total current output of the alternator
the voltage of the electrical system
the current flowing to the starter motor

questions.explanation: A centre-zero ammeter shows the current flowing into or out of the battery. A positive (right) deflection means the battery is being charged by the alternator. A negative (left) deflection means the battery is discharging — more current is being used than the alternator is producing.

questions.question: The pitot tube measures:-

options.text: total pressure (static pressure plus dynamic pressure)

questions.explanation: The pitot tube, facing into the airflow, brings the air to rest at its opening. This captures total (pitot) pressure, which is the sum of static pressure and dynamic pressure. The ASI then subtracts static pressure (from the static port) to determine dynamic pressure, which indicates airspeed.

questions.question: If the pitot tube becomes blocked during flight but the static port remains clear, the ASI will:-

options.text: act like an altimeter — reading increases in a climb and decreases in a descent

questions.explanation: With the pitot tube blocked (and drain hole also blocked), the trapped pitot pressure remains constant. As the aircraft climbs, static pressure decreases — the ASI senses a greater difference (pitot minus static) and over-reads. In a descent, static pressure increases, reducing the difference, and the ASI under-reads. It effectively behaves like an altimeter.

questions.question: Pitot heat is used to:-

options.text: prevent ice from blocking the pitot tube
heat the air entering the carburettor

questions.explanation: Pitot heat is an electrical heating element in the pitot tube that prevents ice from forming over or inside the tube opening. Ice blockage would cause erroneous ASI readings. Pitot heat should be switched on when flying in conditions where icing is possible (visible moisture and temperatures near or below freezing).

questions.question: The altimeter sub-scale (Kollsman window) is used to:-

options.text: set the reference pressure so the altimeter reads the correct altitude
calibrate the instrument for position error

questions.explanation: The sub-scale allows the pilot to set the reference pressure datum. Setting QNH gives altitude above mean sea level. Setting QFE gives height above the aerodrome. Setting 1013.25 hPa gives pressure altitude (flight levels). The correct setting is essential for accurate altitude indication and terrain clearance.

questions.question: When QNH is set on the altimeter sub-scale, the altimeter will indicate:-
questions.explanation: QNH is the atmospheric pressure at mean sea level for a given location. When set on the altimeter, it reads altitude above mean sea level (AMSL). On the ground at the aerodrome, the altimeter should read the aerodrome elevation. QNH is the standard setting for flight below the transition altitude.

questions.question: When QFE is set on the altimeter sub-scale, the altimeter will indicate:-
questions.explanation: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the aerodrome elevation. When set on the altimeter, it reads zero on the ground at that aerodrome and indicates height above the aerodrome during flight. QFE is useful for circuit flying but less common than QNH for general navigation.

questions.question: When 1013.25 hPa is set on the altimeter sub-scale, the altimeter will indicate:-
questions.explanation: Setting 1013.25 hPa (standard pressure) gives pressure altitude — the altitude in the International Standard Atmosphere corresponding to the measured pressure. This is used for flight level assignments above the transition altitude, ensuring all aircraft use the same reference for vertical separation.

questions.question: When flying from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure without adjusting the altimeter sub-scale, the altimeter will:-

options.text: over-read — the aircraft is lower than indicated
under-read — the aircraft is higher than indicated

questions.explanation: Flying from high to low pressure without updating QNH causes the altimeter to over-read (indicate higher than actual altitude). The memory aid is 'High to Low, look out below' — the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter shows, which is dangerous for terrain clearance.

questions.question: When flying from an area of warm air to an area of cold air without adjusting the altimeter, the altimeter will:-

options.text: over-read — the aircraft is lower than indicated
under-read — the aircraft is higher than indicated

questions.explanation: Cold air is denser and the pressure levels are compressed (closer together). The altimeter, calibrated for ISA conditions, will over-read in colder-than-standard conditions. The memory aid is 'Hot to Cold, don't be bold' — the aircraft is lower than indicated. Temperature corrections should be applied in very cold conditions.

questions.question: The VSI operates by measuring:-

options.text: the rate of change of static pressure
the difference between pitot and static pressure
the absolute value of static pressure
the rate of change of pitot pressure

questions.explanation: The VSI measures the rate of change of static pressure. Static pressure is fed directly to a capsule and also to the instrument case through a calibrated leak (metering unit). During a climb or descent, the capsule pressure changes immediately but the case pressure lags, creating a differential proportional to the rate of altitude change.

questions.question: An Instantaneous VSI (IVSI) differs from a conventional VSI in that it:-

options.text: uses accelerometers to provide an immediate response to changes in vertical speed
uses pitot pressure instead of static pressure
does not have a calibrated leak

questions.explanation: The IVSI incorporates small accelerometers (dashpots) that respond immediately to vertical acceleration. This eliminates the lag inherent in a conventional VSI, which must wait for a pressure differential to develop through the calibrated leak. The IVSI provides an almost instantaneous indication of climb or descent.

questions.question: The oil cooler in an engine lubrication system is used to:-

options.text: maintain the oil at the correct operating temperature

questions.explanation: The oil cooler is a heat exchanger (similar to a small radiator) that removes excess heat from the engine oil. Cooling air flows over the cooler, transferring heat from the oil to the atmosphere. Some systems include a thermostat or bypass valve to ensure the oil reaches operating temperature quickly during warm-up.

questions.question: The oil pressure gauge in a wet sump system is usually located in the oil line:-

options.text: between the pressure pump and the engine components

questions.explanation: The oil pressure gauge measures the pressure of oil being delivered to the engine. It is located downstream of the pressure pump and pressure relief valve, in the line feeding oil to the engine bearings and components. This gives the pilot an accurate reading of the oil pressure available for lubrication.

questions.question: A fuel injection system differs from a carburettor system in that:-

options.text: fuel is injected directly into each cylinder intake port
fuel is mixed with air in a venturi
it uses a float chamber to regulate fuel flow
it is more susceptible to icing

questions.explanation: In a fuel injection system, fuel is metered and sprayed directly into each cylinder's intake port (or into the intake manifold near each cylinder). This provides more even fuel distribution, better fuel economy, and reduced susceptibility to icing compared to a carburettor. However, it can be harder to start when hot (vapour lock).

questions.question: The green arc on an airspeed indicator represents:-
questions.explanation: The green arc represents the normal operating speed range. The bottom of the green arc is VS1 (stalling speed in clean configuration) and the top is VNO (maximum structural cruising speed). Flight within the green arc is safe in all conditions including turbulence.

questions.question: The white arc on an airspeed indicator represents:-
questions.explanation: The white arc represents the flap operating range. The bottom is VS0 (stalling speed in landing configuration — full flaps) and the top is VFE (maximum flap extended speed). Flaps should only be extended when the airspeed is within the white arc.

questions.question: The yellow arc on an airspeed indicator represents:-

options.text: the caution range — smooth air only
the best rate of climb speed

questions.explanation: The yellow arc is the caution range, between VNO and VNE. Flight in this range should only be conducted in smooth air and with caution. Turbulence or abrupt control inputs at these speeds could cause structural damage. The top of the yellow arc is the red line (VNE).

questions.question: The red line on an airspeed indicator represents:-

options.text: VNO — the maximum structural cruising speed

questions.explanation: The red line marks VNE (velocity never exceed). Flight at or above this speed risks structural failure. VNE is the absolute maximum speed and must never be exceeded under any circumstances. It is determined during flight testing and includes a safety margin.

questions.question: A Constant Speed Unit (CSU) maintains a constant RPM by:-

options.text: automatically adjusting the propeller blade angle

questions.explanation: The CSU uses a governor with flyweights that sense RPM. If RPM increases above the set value, the governor increases blade angle (coarsens) to absorb more power. If RPM decreases, it decreases blade angle (fines) to reduce the load. This maintains the RPM selected by the pilot on the propeller control.

questions.question: The correct sequence for reducing power in an aeroplane with a CSU is:-

options.text: reduce manifold pressure, reduce RPM, then lean the mixture
reduce RPM, reduce manifold pressure, then lean the mixture
lean the mixture, reduce RPM, then reduce manifold pressure
reduce manifold pressure, lean the mixture, then reduce RPM

questions.explanation: When reducing power: (1) Reduce manifold pressure (throttle back) first to avoid overboosting, (2) Reduce RPM (prop lever back), (3) Lean the mixture as appropriate for the new power setting. This is the reverse of the power increase sequence (mixture, RPM, MP).

questions.question: The compression ratio of a typical aircraft piston engine is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Aircraft piston engines typically have compression ratios of 7:1 to 8.5:1. This is lower than many car engines because aviation fuel (100LL) has a specific octane rating, and higher compression would increase the risk of detonation. Diesel/jet fuel engines have much higher ratios (around 20:1).

questions.question: The purpose of the mixture control is to:-

options.text: adjust the fuel-to-air ratio for different operating conditions

questions.explanation: The mixture control adjusts the ratio of fuel to air entering the engine. At altitude, air density decreases but the carburettor delivers the same fuel volume, making the mixture too rich. The pilot leans the mixture to restore the correct ratio. Full rich is used for take-off and landing; leaned for cruise at altitude.

questions.question: The engine primer is used to:-

options.text: inject fuel directly into the cylinders for cold engine starting

questions.explanation: The primer is a small hand pump that draws fuel from the tank and injects it directly into one or more cylinder intake ports. This provides a combustible mixture for starting a cold engine, when the carburettor cannot vaporise fuel effectively. The primer must be locked after use to prevent it acting as an uncontrolled fuel source.

questions.question: If the primer is left unlocked after engine start, it may cause:-

options.text: an excessively rich mixture and rough running

questions.explanation: An unlocked primer can allow fuel to be drawn through it by engine suction, bypassing the carburettor's metering system. This adds unmetered fuel to the mixture, making it excessively rich. The engine will run rough and may produce black smoke. Always ensure the primer is locked after starting.

questions.question: The function of the oil filter in a lubrication system is to:-

options.text: remove contaminants and metal particles from the oil

questions.explanation: The oil filter removes metal particles, carbon deposits, and other contaminants from the oil before it reaches the engine bearings. A bypass valve allows oil to flow around a blocked filter to prevent oil starvation, though unfiltered. Regular filter changes are part of scheduled maintenance.

questions.question: The brake system on most light aircraft uses:-

options.text: hydraulic disc brakes on the main wheels
pneumatic drum brakes on all wheels

questions.explanation: Most light aircraft use hydraulic disc brakes on the main wheels only (not the nosewheel). The pilot operates them via toe pedals on the rudder pedals. Differential braking (applying more brake on one side) assists in ground steering. A parking brake holds the brakes in the applied position.

questions.question: Differential braking is used to:-

options.text: assist in steering the aircraft on the ground

questions.explanation: Differential braking means applying more brake pressure on one main wheel than the other. This creates a yawing moment that helps steer the aircraft on the ground, particularly useful at low speeds where the rudder and nosewheel steering are less effective, or for tight turns during taxying.

questions.question: An under-inflated tyre may result in:-

options.text: excessive tread wear on the edges of the tyre
excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre

questions.explanation: An under-inflated tyre sags and the edges of the tread bear more of the load, causing them to wear faster than the centre. Under-inflation also increases the risk of tyre creep, generates more heat (risking blowout), and increases rolling resistance during take-off.

questions.question: The purpose of a fuel strainer or gascolator is to:-

options.text: filter contaminants and trap water before fuel reaches the carburettor or fuel injection system

questions.explanation: The fuel strainer (gascolator) is located at the lowest point of the fuel system between the tanks and the engine. It contains a fine mesh screen that filters debris and a bowl that traps water (which is heavier than fuel and settles to the bottom). It has a drain valve for pre-flight sampling.

questions.question: Vapour lock in a fuel system is most likely to occur:-

options.text: in hot weather conditions, particularly with fuel-injected engines

questions.explanation: Vapour lock occurs when fuel vaporises in the fuel lines due to high temperatures, forming gas bubbles that block fuel flow. Fuel-injected engines are more susceptible because fuel lines run close to the hot engine. It is most common during hot weather, after engine shutdown (heat soak), and at high altitude where lower pressure promotes vaporisation.

questions.question: The function of the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) gauge is to:-

options.text: assist the pilot in leaning the mixture for optimum engine efficiency
measure the temperature of the engine cylinders

questions.explanation: The EGT gauge measures the temperature of exhaust gases leaving the cylinders. It is the primary instrument for precise mixture leaning. Peak EGT occurs at stoichiometric mixture. Leaning to peak EGT gives best economy; enrichening 50°F rich of peak gives best power. The EGT also helps detect abnormal combustion.

questions.question: The manifold pressure gauge measures:-

options.text: the absolute pressure of the fuel/air mixture in the intake manifold

questions.explanation: The manifold pressure gauge (MAP) measures the absolute pressure in the engine intake manifold in inches of mercury (inHg). With the engine stopped, it reads atmospheric pressure. During operation, it indicates the power being developed. Higher MAP = more power. It is the primary power indicator on CSU-equipped aircraft.

questions.question: With the engine stopped, the manifold pressure gauge will read approximately:-

options.text: the current atmospheric pressure (about 29.92 inHg at sea level)
the maximum manifold pressure for the engine

questions.explanation: With the engine stopped, the intake manifold is open to the atmosphere through the air intake. The MAP gauge therefore reads atmospheric pressure — approximately 29.92 inHg at sea level in ISA conditions. When the engine is running, the throttle restricts airflow, and MAP drops below atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: A monocoque fuselage structure is one in which:-

options.text: the skin carries all the structural loads
the internal framework carries all loads and the skin is non-structural
formers and stringers carry part of the load with the skin
a truss framework provides all structural strength

questions.explanation: A true monocoque structure relies entirely on the skin to carry all structural loads — bending, torsion, and shear. It has no internal framework. This is strong but heavy (thick skin needed) and vulnerable to dents. Most aircraft use semi-monocoque construction instead, which adds internal formers and stringers to share the load.

questions.question: The function of wing ribs is to:-

options.text: give the wing its aerofoil shape and transfer loads to the spar
provide attachment points for the engine

questions.explanation: Ribs are chordwise structural members that give the wing its aerofoil cross-section shape. They also transfer aerodynamic loads from the skin to the main spar and maintain the shape of the wing under load. They are not the primary load-bearing members — that role belongs to the spar.

questions.question: The function of stringers in a semi-monocoque structure is to:-

options.text: stiffen the skin and carry some of the longitudinal loads
give the fuselage its cross-sectional shape
attach the wings to the fuselage

questions.explanation: Stringers are longitudinal members that run along the length of the fuselage (or wing). They stiffen the skin panels, prevent buckling, and carry some of the longitudinal (bending and compression) loads. They work together with formers (which give the cross-sectional shape) and the stressed skin.

questions.question: The function of formers (frames) in a semi-monocoque structure is to:-

options.text: give the fuselage its cross-sectional shape
provide attachment for the landing gear

questions.explanation: Formers (also called frames or bulkheads) are transverse structural members that define the cross-sectional shape of the fuselage. They support the stringers and skin, distribute concentrated loads (such as from wing or landing gear attachments), and maintain the fuselage shape under load.

questions.question: The ISA (International Standard Atmosphere) sea level temperature is:-
questions.explanation: The ISA defines standard conditions at sea level: temperature 15°C, pressure 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg), density 1.225 kg/m³. Temperature decreases at approximately 1.98°C per 1000 ft (often rounded to 2°C/1000 ft) up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft (-56.5°C).

questions.question: The ISA sea level pressure is:-
questions.explanation: The ISA standard sea level pressure is 1013.25 hPa (hectopascals), equivalent to 29.92 inches of mercury (inHg) or 14.7 psi. This is the reference pressure used for pressure altitude and flight level calculations. It is set on the altimeter sub-scale when flying at or above the transition altitude.

questions.question: The ISA temperature lapse rate in the troposphere is approximately:-
questions.explanation: In the ISA, temperature decreases at 1.98°C per 1000 ft (often rounded to 2°C/1000 ft) from sea level up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft. Above the tropopause, temperature remains constant at -56.5°C in the ISA model. This lapse rate is used for all standard atmosphere calculations.

questions.question: The ISA density of air at sea level is:-
questions.explanation: The ISA standard sea level air density is 1.225 kg/m³ (or 1225 g/m³). Air density decreases with altitude, increasing temperature, and increasing humidity. Density is critical because it directly affects lift, drag, engine power output, and propeller efficiency.

questions.question: The tachometer on a piston-engine aircraft indicates:-
questions.explanation: The tachometer measures and displays engine revolutions per minute (RPM). On a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft, RPM is the primary power indicator. On a CSU-equipped aircraft, RPM is set by the propeller control and manifold pressure is the primary power indicator.

questions.question: The fuel selector valve on a typical light aircraft allows the pilot to:-

options.text: select which fuel tank supplies fuel to the engine
drain water from the fuel tanks

questions.explanation: The fuel selector valve allows the pilot to choose which tank feeds the engine — typically LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH, or OFF. Proper fuel management (switching tanks periodically) maintains lateral balance and ensures all available fuel is used. The OFF position is used for engine shutdown and emergencies.

questions.question: An electric fuel pump is typically used:-

options.text: as a backup to the engine-driven fuel pump and for engine starting
as the primary fuel pump during cruise

questions.explanation: The electric (auxiliary) fuel pump provides fuel pressure for engine starting (before the engine-driven pump is operating) and serves as a backup if the engine-driven pump fails. It is also used during take-off and landing as a precaution, and to purge vapour from fuel lines in hot conditions.

questions.question: The electrical bus (busbar) in an aircraft is:-

options.text: a common distribution point for electrical power to all circuits

questions.explanation: The electrical bus (busbar) is a central distribution bar or terminal strip to which the battery, alternator/generator, and all electrical circuits are connected. It provides a common point for distributing electrical power. Some aircraft have multiple buses (essential and non-essential) for load shedding in emergencies.

questions.question: The purpose of an ELT (Emergency Locator Transmitter) is to:-

options.text: transmit a distress signal on emergency frequencies to aid search and rescue

questions.explanation: The ELT automatically activates on impact (or can be manually activated) and transmits a distress signal on 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz. The 406 MHz signal is detected by COSPAS-SARSAT satellites, which relay the aircraft's position to rescue coordination centres. It is a critical survival aid.

questions.question: A transponder in Mode C transmits:-

options.text: the aircraft's identification code and pressure altitude

questions.explanation: Mode C transponder transmits the aircraft's squawk code (4-digit identification) and pressure altitude (from the encoding altimeter). This allows ATC radar to display both the aircraft's identity and altitude. Mode A transmits the squawk code only (no altitude). Mode S provides additional data capabilities.

questions.question: Control cables in an aircraft are typically made of:-
questions.explanation: Flight control cables are made of stainless steel wire rope for strength, flexibility, and corrosion resistance. They are typically 7x7 or 7x19 construction (7 strands of 7 or 19 wires each). Cable tension must be checked regularly as it changes with temperature — cables tighten in cold weather and loosen in hot weather.

questions.question: A split flap differs from a plain flap in that:-

options.text: only the lower surface of the trailing edge deflects downward
the entire trailing edge deflects downward
it slides rearward and then deflects
it has a slot between the flap and the wing

questions.explanation: A split flap is hinged at the lower surface of the trailing edge — only the lower portion deflects downward while the upper surface remains in place. This produces more drag than a plain flap (where the entire trailing edge deflects) but a similar increase in lift. Split flaps are simple and effective speed brakes.

questions.question: A Fowler flap increases lift more effectively than other flap types because:-

options.text: it increases both the wing area and the camber
it deflects further than other flap types

questions.explanation: A Fowler flap first slides rearward (increasing the effective wing area) and then deflects downward (increasing camber). This double action produces a greater increase in CL than plain or split flaps at the same deflection angle, making it the most aerodynamically efficient flap type for increasing lift.

questions.question: A slotted flap improves performance over a plain flap because:-

options.text: the slot directs high-energy air over the flap surface, delaying separation
it is lighter than a plain flap
it does not change the wing camber

questions.explanation: A slotted flap has a gap (slot) between the wing and the flap. When deflected, high-pressure air from below flows through the slot over the upper surface of the flap, energising the boundary layer and delaying flow separation. This allows greater flap deflection before the flow separates, producing more lift.

questions.question: The Hobbs meter in an aircraft records:-

options.text: the total time the engine has been running or the aircraft has been in use

questions.explanation: The Hobbs meter is a running-time recorder that typically activates when the master switch is on or when oil pressure is present (engine running). It records total operating time in hours and tenths. This time is used for maintenance scheduling, rental billing, and logbook entries.
