questions.question: The purpose of a fuel vent on an aircraft fuel tank is to:-

options.text: allow air to enter the tank as fuel is consumed, preventing a vacuum
release fuel vapour to reduce fire risk

questions.explanation: As fuel is consumed, the volume in the tank must be replaced by air. Without a vent, a vacuum would form, eventually stopping fuel flow to the engine. The vent also allows air to escape during refuelling and allows for thermal expansion of fuel. A blocked vent can cause engine fuel starvation.

questions.question: The gyro erection mechanism in an attitude indicator is designed to:-

options.text: keep the gyro aligned with the earth's vertical
align the gyro with magnetic north

questions.explanation: The erection mechanism uses pendulous vanes (in vacuum-driven instruments) or torque motors (in electric instruments) to continuously correct the gyro back to the true vertical. Without it, friction and other forces would cause the gyro to drift from the vertical over time, giving incorrect attitude indications.

questions.question: The magnetic compass is subject to turning errors because:-

options.text: the compass magnet assembly is free to dip toward the nearer magnetic pole
the compass fluid is affected by temperature
the compass card is not perfectly balanced
the earth's magnetic field is uniform

questions.explanation: The compass magnet assembly is suspended on a pivot and is free to dip toward the nearer magnetic pole (magnetic dip). During turns, the banking of the aircraft tilts the pivot, and the dipping magnet causes the compass to give erroneous readings. These errors are most pronounced on northerly and southerly headings.

questions.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, when turning through north using only the magnetic compass:-

options.text: the compass lags behind the actual heading
the compass leads the actual heading

questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, the compass lags when turning through north and leads when turning through south. The memory aid for the Southern Hemisphere is: through North = lag (undershoot, roll out past the desired heading on the compass); through South = lead (overshoot, roll out before the desired heading).

questions.question: The purpose of the compass correction card is to:-

options.text: show the deviation on various headings so the pilot can steer the correct compass heading
show the variation for the area

questions.explanation: The compass correction card (deviation card) is placed near the compass and lists the deviation for headings at regular intervals (typically every 30°). The pilot uses it to determine what compass heading to steer to achieve the desired magnetic heading. It is updated after each compass swing.

questions.question: The purpose of the oil in a wet sump lubrication system includes:-
questions.explanation: Engine oil serves four main functions: (1) Lubrication — reduces friction between moving parts, (2) Cooling — absorbs and carries away heat from engine components, (3) Cleaning — carries contaminants to the filter, (4) Sealing — helps seal the gap between piston rings and cylinder walls to maintain compression.

questions.question: High oil pressure coupled with low oil temperature on engine start indicates:-

options.text: normal operation — the oil is cold and viscous

questions.explanation: When the engine is first started, the oil is cold and thick (high viscosity). Cold, viscous oil resists flow, causing higher pressure readings. As the engine warms up, the oil thins, flows more easily, and the pressure drops to the normal operating range. This is normal and expected.

questions.question: If the rotor speed of a turn indicator increases above normal, the pointer will:-

options.text: show a lesser rate of turn than actual
show a higher rate of turn than actual

questions.explanation: A faster-spinning gyro has greater rigidity in space and resists precession more strongly. For a given rate of turn, the gyro precesses less against the calibrated spring, resulting in less needle deflection. The instrument under-reads — it shows a lesser rate of turn than the aircraft is actually making.

questions.question: The spark plugs in an aircraft engine are typically:-

options.text: two per cylinder — one fired by each magneto

questions.explanation: Each cylinder has two spark plugs, one connected to the left magneto and one to the right. This provides redundancy (engine runs on one magneto if the other fails) and more efficient combustion (two flame fronts burn the mixture faster and more completely than one).

questions.question: The magneto ignition switch positions are typically:-
questions.explanation: The standard magneto switch has five positions: OFF (both magnetos grounded), RIGHT (right magneto only), LEFT (left magneto only), BOTH (both magnetos active — normal operation), and START (engages the starter motor while on BOTH). The switch grounds magnetos to stop them, rather than powering them.

questions.question: The engine-driven fuel pump in a carburettor-equipped aircraft is typically a:-
questions.explanation: The engine-driven fuel pump is typically a diaphragm type, operated by an eccentric cam on the engine accessory drive. It provides a steady, low-pressure fuel supply to the carburettor. The diaphragm design is simple, reliable, and self-regulating — it stops pumping when the carburettor float bowl is full.

questions.question: The function of the throttle in a carburettor is to:-

options.text: control the amount of fuel/air mixture entering the engine by varying the butterfly valve opening

questions.explanation: The throttle controls a butterfly valve in the carburettor venturi. Opening the throttle opens the butterfly valve, allowing more fuel/air mixture to flow into the engine, increasing power. Closing it restricts the flow, reducing power. The throttle controls the quantity of mixture, not the ratio (that is the mixture control's job).

questions.question: In a float-type carburettor, the float mechanism controls:-

options.text: the fuel level in the float chamber by opening and closing the needle valve
the air flow through the venturi

questions.explanation: The float rises and falls with the fuel level in the float chamber. When the fuel level drops, the float lowers and opens the needle valve, allowing fuel to flow in from the pump. When the level is correct, the float rises and closes the valve. This maintains a constant fuel level for consistent metering.

questions.question: The venturi in a carburettor causes fuel to be drawn from the float chamber because:-

options.text: the air accelerating through the venturi creates a low pressure area
the fuel pump pushes fuel into the venturi
gravity feeds fuel from the float chamber

questions.explanation: As air flows through the narrowed venturi section, it accelerates and the static pressure drops (Bernoulli's principle). The fuel discharge nozzle is located at the throat of the venturi where pressure is lowest. The pressure difference between the float chamber (atmospheric) and the venturi throat draws fuel out and atomises it into the airstream.

questions.question: Carburettor icing can occur at ambient temperatures as high as:-
questions.explanation: The temperature drop in the carburettor (from the venturi effect and fuel evaporation) can be 20-30°C. This means ice can form even when the outside air temperature is as high as +25°C, provided humidity is high enough. The most dangerous conditions are temperatures between -5°C and +20°C with visible moisture or high humidity.

questions.question: When carburettor heat is applied and ice is present, the pilot should expect:-

options.text: an initial further drop in RPM followed by a gradual increase as the ice melts

questions.explanation: Applying carburettor heat initially causes a further RPM drop because the warm air is less dense (richens the mixture, reduces power). As the heat melts the ice, the water passes through the engine causing temporary rough running. Then RPM gradually increases as the ice clears and normal airflow is restored.

questions.question: The advantage of a retractable undercarriage over a fixed undercarriage is:-

options.text: reduced parasite drag in flight, resulting in higher cruise speed

questions.explanation: Retracting the landing gear removes it from the airflow, significantly reducing parasite (form) drag. This allows higher cruise speeds for the same power setting, or the same speed with less fuel burn. The disadvantage is added weight, complexity, cost, and the risk of a gear-up landing.

questions.question: The green light in a landing gear indicator system indicates:-

options.text: the gear is down and locked
the gear is up and locked

questions.explanation: Landing gear indication typically uses: green = gear down and locked (safe to land), red = gear in transit or unsafe, no light = gear up and locked (in some systems). Three green lights (one per gear leg) confirm all gear are down and locked before landing.

questions.question: The purpose of a squat switch (weight-on-wheels switch) is to:-

options.text: prevent certain systems from operating when the aircraft is on the ground or in the air

questions.explanation: The squat switch detects whether the aircraft is on the ground (weight on wheels) or airborne. It is used to prevent inadvertent gear retraction on the ground, enable ground-only systems (e.g., nosewheel steering), and activate air-only systems. It is typically mounted on the main gear oleo strut.

questions.question: The trim tab on a control surface works by:-

options.text: creating an aerodynamic force that holds the control surface in the desired position
changing the shape of the wing

questions.explanation: A trim tab is a small hinged surface on the trailing edge of a primary control surface. When deflected, it creates an aerodynamic force on the control surface that holds it in the desired position without the pilot needing to maintain constant pressure on the controls. This reduces pilot workload during sustained flight conditions.

questions.question: To trim the aircraft nose-up, the elevator trim tab must be deflected:-
questions.explanation: The trim tab moves in the opposite direction to the desired control surface movement. To trim nose-up, the elevator must move up. The trim tab deflects down, which creates a downward aerodynamic force on the tab that pushes the elevator trailing edge up. This is why the trim wheel direction may seem counterintuitive.

questions.question: An anti-servo tab (anti-balance tab) on a stabilator:-

options.text: moves in the same direction as the control surface to increase control forces
moves in the opposite direction to reduce control forces

questions.explanation: An anti-servo tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator (all-moving tailplane). When the stabilator deflects trailing edge up, the tab also deflects up. This creates an opposing aerodynamic force that makes the controls feel heavier, preventing the stabilator from being too sensitive. It also serves as a trim tab.

questions.question: A balance tab (servo tab) on a control surface:-

options.text: moves in the opposite direction to the control surface to reduce control forces
moves in the same direction to increase control forces

questions.explanation: A balance (servo) tab moves in the opposite direction to the control surface. When the elevator deflects up, the balance tab deflects down. The aerodynamic force on the tab assists the pilot in moving the control surface, reducing the stick force required. This is particularly useful on larger aircraft.

questions.question: Mass balancing of control surfaces is used to:-

options.text: prevent flutter by moving the centre of gravity of the surface forward of the hinge line
reduce the weight of the control surface

questions.explanation: Flutter is a dangerous oscillation that can destroy a control surface. It occurs when the CG of the surface is behind the hinge line. Mass balancing adds weight ahead of the hinge line (often as a lead weight in the leading edge or on a horn) to move the CG forward, preventing flutter.

questions.question: If both the pitot tube and its drain hole become blocked simultaneously during level flight, the ASI will:-

options.text: freeze at the current reading and then behave like an altimeter

questions.explanation: With both the pitot opening and drain hole blocked, the pitot pressure is trapped at its current value. In level flight at constant speed, the ASI initially reads correctly. But if altitude changes, the static pressure changes while pitot stays trapped — the ASI then acts like an altimeter (over-reads in a climb, under-reads in a descent).

questions.question: If the pitot tube becomes blocked but the drain hole remains open, the ASI will:-

options.text: gradually drop to zero as the trapped pressure equalises through the drain

questions.explanation: If only the pitot opening is blocked but the drain hole is open, the ram air pressure trapped in the pitot line will slowly leak out through the drain hole. The pitot pressure will equalise with static pressure, and since ASI reads the difference (pitot minus static), the reading will gradually drop to zero.

questions.question: Calibrated airspeed (CAS) is obtained by correcting IAS for:-
questions.explanation: CAS = IAS corrected for instrument error (inaccuracies in the ASI mechanism) and position error (caused by the location of the pitot tube and static ports on the aircraft, which may not sense true undisturbed pressures in all flight conditions). CAS is then corrected for density to obtain TAS.

questions.question: True airspeed (TAS) is obtained by correcting CAS for:-
questions.explanation: TAS = CAS corrected for non-standard air density (temperature and pressure). At altitude, air is less dense, so the aircraft must fly faster (higher TAS) to produce the same dynamic pressure (same IAS/CAS). TAS is the actual speed of the aircraft through the air mass and is used for navigation calculations.

questions.question: The engine cooling system on most light aircraft is:-

options.text: air-cooled, using ram air directed over finned cylinders by baffles

questions.explanation: Most light aircraft piston engines are air-cooled. Ram air enters through the cowling inlet, is directed over the finned cylinder barrels and heads by baffles and deflectors, absorbs heat, and exits through the cowl flaps or rear of the cowling. This system is lighter and simpler than liquid cooling.

questions.question: Engine overheating is most likely to occur during:-

options.text: a prolonged climb at high power with low airspeed

questions.explanation: During a prolonged climb, the engine is producing high power (generating lots of heat) but the airspeed is relatively low (less cooling air flowing over the cylinders). This combination of high heat production and reduced cooling is the most common cause of engine overheating. Opening cowl flaps and enrichening the mixture helps.

questions.question: Shock cooling of an engine can occur when:-

options.text: power is reduced rapidly and the aircraft descends quickly in cold air
the engine is started in cold weather
the mixture is leaned at altitude

questions.explanation: Shock cooling occurs when engine temperatures drop too rapidly — typically during a rapid descent at low power in cold air. The cylinders cool faster than the pistons (which retain heat longer), causing differential contraction that can crack cylinders. Avoid rapid power reductions and descend with partial power to prevent this.

questions.question: The purpose of the oil bypass valve (oil filter bypass) is to:-

options.text: allow oil to bypass a blocked filter to prevent oil starvation

questions.explanation: If the oil filter becomes blocked (by contaminants or cold, thick oil), the bypass valve opens to allow unfiltered oil to reach the engine components. While unfiltered oil is not ideal, it is far better than no oil at all. The bypass valve prevents engine seizure due to oil starvation from a blocked filter.

questions.question: The advantage of a horizontally opposed engine layout used in most light aircraft is:-

options.text: low frontal area, good balance, and smooth operation

questions.explanation: Horizontally opposed (flat) engines have cylinders arranged in two banks on opposite sides of the crankcase. This gives a low frontal area (less drag), good natural balance (opposing pistons cancel vibrations), a flat profile that allows good forward visibility, and a low centre of gravity. Most Lycoming and Continental engines use this layout.

questions.question: The function of the crankshaft in a piston engine is to:-

options.text: convert the reciprocating motion of the pistons into rotary motion

questions.explanation: The crankshaft converts the linear (reciprocating) motion of the pistons into rotary motion to drive the propeller. The connecting rods link the pistons to the crankshaft throws (offset journals). The crankshaft also drives the camshaft, magnetos, oil pump, fuel pump, and other accessories through gears.

questions.question: The camshaft in a piston engine controls:-

options.text: the opening and closing of the inlet and exhaust valves

questions.explanation: The camshaft has lobes (cams) that push against the valve lifters (tappets), opening the inlet and exhaust valves at the correct time in the engine cycle. The camshaft is driven by the crankshaft at half crankshaft speed (one camshaft revolution per two crankshaft revolutions in a four-stroke engine).

questions.question: The function of piston rings is to:-

options.text: seal the combustion chamber and control oil consumption
connect the piston to the crankshaft
reduce the weight of the piston

questions.explanation: Piston rings serve two main purposes: compression rings seal the gap between the piston and cylinder wall to prevent combustion gases from escaping into the crankcase (blow-by), and oil control rings scrape excess oil from the cylinder wall and return it to the sump, preventing oil from entering the combustion chamber.

questions.question: The connecting rod in a piston engine connects:-

options.text: the magneto to the spark plugs

questions.explanation: The connecting rod (con rod) links the piston to the crankshaft. The small end connects to the piston via the gudgeon (wrist) pin, and the big end connects to the crankshaft throw via a bearing. It transmits the force from the expanding gases acting on the piston to the crankshaft, converting linear motion to rotary motion.
